subject: ela
intro: Plot is the sequence of events in a story, organized as rising action (the conflict builds), a climax (the turning point), and falling action leading to resolution. Characters change or stay the same as the plot unfolds, and understanding how a character responds to events reveals who they are. In grade 6, you will analyze both how a plot develops through episodes and how characters change across those episodes.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

At the start of the school year, Marcus sat alone at lunch every day, not because he had no one to sit with, but because he preferred it. He listened to music and drew in a sketchbook. He had always been like this.

In January, a new student named Dara sat down across from him without asking. He kept drawing. She kept sitting there. The next day she sat there again.

By March, they were talking every lunch period. By May, Marcus realized he had been happier with someone to talk to than he had admitted to himself.

Describe how Marcus changes over the course of the plot. What specific events cause or reveal his change?

steps: Identify Marcus's initial state: deliberately solitary, 'he preferred it.'
Identify the event that disrupts this: Dara sits down uninvited.
Trace the change through specific plot points: January sitting, March talking, May realization.
Describe what he learns about himself by the end.
solution.answer: At the start, Marcus is described as preferring isolation, sitting alone not from exclusion but choice. He represents someone who has built a settled identity around solitude. The disrupting event is Dara sitting down without permission in January. He does not engage but also does not leave. By March, they are talking every lunch, which marks a behavioral change. The most significant moment is in May, when he realizes he had been 'happier with someone to talk to than he had admitted to himself.' This is a self-aware change: he recognizes not just that his behavior changed but that his earlier self-concept had been incomplete. The plot drives him from a defended isolation to an acknowledged need for connection.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The story of Mira's first year at the new school had three distinct phases.

In September, she was invisible: no one spoke to her, she did not speak to anyone. She ate lunch quickly and hid in the library for the rest of the period.

In November, after she corrected a mistake in the class presentation, the teacher asked her to lead the next one. She spent two weeks dreading it and then did it anyway.

By February, she was the one other students asked when they were confused. She still preferred the library at lunch, but now she went there by choice rather than by hiding.

Describe how the plot of Mira's first year unfolds in episodes and how her character changes across them.

steps: Identify the three episodes: September (invisible), November (reluctant visibility), February (respected).
Identify what changes within Mira: her agency and her relationship to choice.
Connect each episode to the previous one as cause and effect.
Note what stays the same: her preference for the library.
solution.answer: The plot unfolds in three distinct episodes. In September, Mira is passive: invisible by default, hiding in the library from necessity. In November, she is pulled into visibility against her will when her correction is noticed; the two weeks of dread shows the episode costs her, but she completes it anyway. By February, the consequences of that choice have accumulated: she is now sought out by other students. The character change across these episodes is her shift from involuntary invisibility to acknowledged competence. Importantly, the library preference remains: she still goes there at lunch. But 'now she went there by choice rather than by hiding.' This detail shows the change is not about becoming a different person but about gaining agency over the same preferences she always had.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The summer cabin had been in the family for forty years. Every July, all three cousins came. For the first twenty years, they had been children together. For the last twenty, they had been adults who kept coming back out of habit.

This July was different. Grandma Rosa had died in April. The cabin would be sold at the end of August.

The first two days were quiet. Everyone cleaned something that didn't need cleaning. On the third day, Lucia found the old box of photos and called the others in. They stayed there until midnight, telling the same stories, laughing at the same moments.

How does the setting and the change in circumstances affect how the characters behave? Trace the plot's development.

steps: Identify the setting's significance: forty-year family cabin, going to be sold.
Identify the plot shift: Grandma Rosa's death changes the July visit.
Trace the character behavior in phases: two days of avoidance, then the discovery of the photos.
Explain how the photo box becomes the turning point in the plot.
solution.answer: The setting is central to this plot: the cabin has forty years of accumulated family meaning, and its imminent sale makes this July the last. The death of Grandma Rosa has changed the emotional stakes of the gathering. The plot begins with avoidance: everyone cleans things that don't need cleaning, which is displacement activity, occupying themselves with tasks that substitute for acknowledging grief. The turning point is Lucia's discovery of the photo box on the third day, which reorients the characters from avoidance to memory. They stay until midnight telling old stories. The setting, a cabin full of forty years of shared history, enables this turn: the box of photos could only exist here. The characters use the last visit to do what the cabin was always for: hold the family together in a shared narrative.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For the first three chapters of the story, we see Kenji only through other characters' eyes: his mother who thinks he works too hard, his teacher who thinks he is lazy, his best friend who thinks he is secretly funny.

In chapter four, we get Kenji's own chapter. He is afraid of failing. He tells jokes to avoid looking serious. He stays up late not because he is working but because he is afraid to stop.

How does the plot's structure, moving from outside views to Kenji's own perspective, affect how we understand his character development?

steps: Describe what we know in chapters 1-3: three contradictory outside views.
Describe what chapter 4 reveals: Kenji's interior, which explains all three outside views.
Explain how the structure itself creates the character development.
Connect specific earlier details to the interior revelations.
solution.answer: For three chapters, Kenji is seen only from outside, and the three views contradict each other: his mother sees hard work, his teacher sees laziness, his friend sees secret humor. This creates a character who seems defined by others' projections. Chapter four performs the plot's central reversal: we enter Kenji's perspective, and the contradictions resolve into a coherent interior. He stays up late not from work ethic or laziness but from fear of stopping. He tells jokes not because he is funny by nature but to avoid looking serious. The structure itself creates the character development: the reader's understanding of Kenji doesn't change because Kenji changes, but because we finally have access to him. The shift from external to internal perspective is the plot's climax.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

When they found the old woman's journal in her desk after she passed, her daughter expected to find things she didn't know. She read for three hours.

Almost everything in it she already knew. The worries were familiar. The small joys were ones she had heard described before. The only thing that surprised her was a section near the end where her mother had written: 'I think she doesn't know how much she has always been exactly what I hoped for.'

The daughter closed the journal and sat there for a long time.

Describe how the plot of this passage moves toward its resolution and how the daughter's character is affected by the climactic discovery.

steps: Identify the setup: the daughter expects to learn something new from the journal.
Identify the complication: most of the journal is already familiar.
Identify the climax: the unexpected sentence about herself.
Describe the resolution: she closes the journal and sits still.
solution.answer: The plot turns on the daughter's expectation of discovery. She opens the journal hoping to learn things she did not know, which implies she expects some gap in her knowledge of her mother. The complication is that the journal confirms rather than reveals: the worries and joys are already familiar. The climax is the one thing that is unexpected: her mother's written statement that she, the daughter, had always been exactly what she had hoped for. This is not information about the mother but about the daughter as seen by the mother. The character impact is significant: she closes the journal and sits still, a response that shows the sentence has reached something deep. The resolution is quiet but complete. She does not need more information. The journal has given her something she did not know she was looking for.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

In the first week of the camping trip, the five teenagers barely spoke. They had been assigned as a group by the program. They did their required tasks separately, ate quickly, went to their separate tents.

In the second week, their assigned guide got sick and had to leave. No replacement came. They had to navigate on their own.

By the third week, they had divided responsibilities naturally, without arguing: two navigated, two cooked, one handled the gear. They had developed a system without deciding to.

Describe how the plot unfolds in episodes and how the characters change across them.
items.hint: Think about what forces the change and what the characters' behavior at the end says about who they have become.

steps: Episode 1: assigned group, avoidance, parallel function.
Episode 2: guide leaves; forced necessity.
Episode 3: natural system develops without conscious decision.
Change: they go from strangers organized by external assignment to a functional unit organized by internal agreement.
solution.answer: The plot unfolds across three episodes. In week one, the five teens are a group only by assignment, functioning in parallel without real collaboration. The plot's turning point is the guide's departure: external authority is removed and necessity fills its place. In week three, they have self-organized into a working unit. The most revealing detail is that the system developed 'without deciding to.' They did not hold a meeting or assign roles. Character change is shown through this organic emergence: they have moved from enforced proximity to genuine cooperation, not through deliberate effort but through shared experience of necessity. The guide's absence is the plot's central episode because it removes the external structure that was preventing internal structure from forming.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The old detective had solved over three hundred cases in thirty years. In every one, she had followed the evidence wherever it led, even when it led somewhere she didn't want to go.

The hardest case of her career was the last one: the man the evidence pointed to was her former partner.

She closed the case. She handed in the file. She retired the following week without explanation.

Describe how the plot moves toward resolution and how the detective's character is revealed through her response to the climax.
items.hint: Think about what the 'hardest case' reveals about who she is and what costs her most.

steps: Establish her established character: three hundred cases, follows evidence wherever it leads.
Identify the climax: the evidence points to her former partner.
Trace her response: she closes the case, files it, retires.
Analyze what the response reveals about her.
solution.answer: The plot builds on the detective's established identity: she has spent thirty years following evidence wherever it leads, even 'when it led somewhere she didn't want to go.' This detail prepares us for the climax. The hardest case tests this exact principle when the evidence points to someone she cares about. Her response shows that her identity holds: she closes the case and hands in the file. She does not suppress evidence or protect her partner. But the retirement immediately after, 'without explanation,' reveals the cost. She has done what her career demanded, but she cannot continue the career after it has required this. The plot resolution is not triumphant. It is the act of a person who honored her values at the highest personal cost and then chose not to remain in the world that cost them.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Marcella had not spoken to her grandmother in four years after an argument about her choices. She had been right. She had known she was right.

When she learned her grandmother was in the hospital, she drove three hours. She sat by the bed. Her grandmother was asleep. Marcella sat there anyway.

When her grandmother woke up, she said, 'I didn't think you'd come.'

Marcella said, 'I almost didn't.'

Describe the plot development of this passage and what the climactic exchange reveals about both characters.
items.hint: The exchange in the last two lines is the climax. What does each line reveal about each person?

steps: Setup: four-year silence, Marcella was right, knew it.
Inciting event: grandmother's hospitalization.
Rising action: three-hour drive, sitting by sleeping bed.
Climax: the two-line exchange at waking.
What each line reveals.
solution.answer: The plot is compressed but structured around the central tension: Marcella has been right and has maintained her position for four years. The inciting event is the hospitalization, which forces her to choose between being right and being present. The three-hour drive and the bedside waiting are the rising action. The climax is the exchange. The grandmother's 'I didn't think you'd come' reveals she had not expected to be chosen over the argument. Marcella's 'I almost didn't' is equally revealing: she is not pretending the four years didn't happen or that the wrong is forgiven. She acknowledges the cost of coming. The exchange is the most honest possible resolution: two people with unresolved grievances choosing each other anyway, without erasing what happened.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

At the beginning of the story, twelve-year-old Sam believed that being the best at something meant doing it alone. He never asked for help. He read instructions once and refused to look at them again. He considered asking for help a form of failure.

In the middle of the story, the science fair project he had been building alone for two months collapsed the night before the fair. With twelve hours left, he called his lab partner, who had offered to help three times before.

They stayed up until 3 a.m. and finished it.

At the end, Sam won second place. He thanked his partner in his speech.

Describe how Sam changes over the course of this plot. Which episode is the turning point and why?
items.hint: Look at what Sam believed at the start versus what his final action shows.

steps: Start: Sam believes excellence requires independence; asking for help = failure.
Turning point: project collapses, forcing him to choose between his belief and the goal.
End: acknowledges partner publicly.
Analyze what the public thanks reveals about his change.
solution.answer: Sam begins the story with a belief that excellence and independence are the same thing. This belief is the internal antagonist, not another character. The turning point is the collapse of the project the night before: the crisis strips away the option of maintaining both excellence and independence. By calling his partner, he accepts help for the first time, but this is still private. The most significant moment of character change is the public thanks in his speech. Winning second place while acknowledging a partner is the complete inversion of his opening belief: he demonstrates that the work succeeded because he allowed collaboration. Thanking his partner publicly means accepting that his identity as 'the best' is no longer built on solitary effort. The plot has moved him from a defended isolation to an expressed gratitude.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The two sisters had been building the same sandcastle every summer at the beach since they were five. They had always built it the same way: four towers, a moat, a drawbridge made of sticks.

This summer, the younger sister was thirteen. She wanted to try something different, a modern design with no moat. The older sister said no.

They built two separate castles. By the time the tide came in, neither had spoken. The older sister watched both castles dissolve.

'Next year we should try your design,' she said.

Describe the plot development and how the older sister's character changes by the resolution.
items.hint: Look at what the older sister chooses at the end and what it costs her.

steps: Setup: eight years of the same design, tradition as identity.
Conflict: younger sister wants change, older sister refuses.
Climax: they build separately, silence, watch both dissolve.
Resolution: older sister's offer.
Character change: from defending tradition to offering to honor change.
solution.answer: The plot builds around tradition as identity: the same castle design for eight years is not just a beach activity but a form of shared ritual. The younger sister's desire to change the design is the conflict, and the older sister's refusal preserves the ritual at the cost of the relationship. The climax is the two separate castles dissolving together, with neither sister speaking. The tide erases both the traditional design and the modern one equally. The resolution is the older sister's offer to try the new design next year. This is a significant character change: she was the one who refused to change, and she makes the offer after watching her own castle dissolve anyway. The tide is the neutral agent that levels the argument. Her offer shows she has understood that the ritual is less important than the person she builds it with.
